Monday: Our student team presented a model of a parcel locker for an apartment building. We had spent hours making the screen bright and the symbols attractive. During a demonstration, a resident praised the display, then set her shopping bags on the floor before opening a door. We assumed the door needed a stronger motor. She explained that she had put down her bags because she could not tell where to pull.
Wednesday: We replaced the working screen with a printed sheet and built several cardboard door handles. This rough model let us change parts between tests instead of waiting for new electronic components. We asked residents to collect a parcel while carrying their usual belongings. A handle that seemed obvious to us disappeared from view behind a full shopping bag. A colored arrow helped people find it, but the narrow grip remained difficult to hold.

The caretaker asked whether we were ready to install the final version. I wanted to say yes, especially after all the work we had done. Instead, we arranged another test with delivery workers, whose gloves might create different difficulties. Our first assumption had sent us toward a stronger motor; watching someone use the locker had sent us toward a different handle. I no longer wanted to treat a successful demonstration as the end of the investigation.
q: Which statement best describes how the diary develops?
choices: A series of tests confirms the first motor theory.
Repeated observations lead to a revised design.
An attractive display solves a problem with doors.
An improved model removes the need for more tests.

An undo button makes a screen feel forgiving. Delete the wrong sentence, restore it, and nothing seems lost. That experience can encourage us to experiment. Trouble begins when we expect a shared digital space to be equally easy to repair. Consider a music club that manages its rehearsal schedule online. Its secretary accidentally removes Friday's rehearsal, and the system immediately sends a cancellation message to every member.
The secretary notices the mistake and presses undo. Friday's rehearsal appears on the calendar again. Yet one member has already accepted a work shift, and another has arranged to meet a friend. The screen has returned to its earlier state; their plans have not. A correction message helps, but it cannot ensure that everyone will read it before making other arrangements. Restoring a record and restoring the situation it created are different tasks.
Should the club therefore remove the undo button? That would make correction harder without preventing the original error. A better approach would let the secretary preview schedule changes before releasing them to members. The system could also make clear when a change has already produced a public message. People should not have to guess whether they are revising a private draft or taking an action others will respond to.
The lesson reaches beyond rehearsal calendars. Digital tools should make mistakes easier to correct, while honestly showing which effects cannot be taken back. An undo button is valuable, but it should invite careful exploration rather than promise that every action leaves no trace.
q: Which statement best expresses the writer's view of undo buttons?
choices: They make shared calendars too risky to use.
They restore members' plans after corrections.
They help when their limits are made clear.
They make a preview of shared changes unnecessary.
explain: 作者肯定撤回功能，也要求呈現不能復原的影響。復原行事曆不代表成員的行程能復原；因此仍建議公開變更前先預覽。

Monday, April 6. My drawing notebook now has a calendar inside its cover. Every evening I sketch one object on the kitchen table, then color a square. At first, the growing line of squares pleased me more than the drawings. I kept checking how many days I had managed without a break. If I missed an evening, I planned to draw twice as long the next day to make up for it.
Thursday, April 16. A weekend visit to my cousins left two empty squares. Back home, I looked at the broken line and put the notebook away. The next evening, I wanted to sketch a spoon, but starting again seemed pointless: my longest run was already ruined. Three more evenings passed before I noticed that the calendar, which was meant to help me draw, had become a reason to avoid drawing.
Tuesday, April 21. Yesterday I drew the spoon for five minutes. I left the empty squares as they were and added a small arrow beside the new sketch. The arrow means I came back. I will still record my evenings, but I want to notice returns as well as long runs. My drawings have not suddenly become better. Yet tonight I opened the notebook without calculating how much work I owed it.

A Drawing Calendar Gets a New Purpose
A Month of Steady Artistic Improvement

subject: english
passage:
Dear Advice Desk: Whenever my friend complains about her weekend job, I offer a plan. I have suggested changing shifts, speaking to her manager, and finding another job. She rejects each idea and recently said I was not listening. But I remember every problem she mentions. How can she say that? Signed, Puzzled.
Dear Puzzled: Remembering the facts is one part of listening. Finding out what the speaker needs is another. Your friend may be trying to describe a difficult day before she decides whether anything needs to change. An immediate plan can leave that part of the conversation unfinished. She may feel dismissed even when you have correctly understood the events.
Next time, briefly reflect what you heard: "It sounds as though you felt left out when the schedule changed." Then check whether that is accurate. You might also ask, "Would you like ideas, or would it help to talk this through?" Neither question requires you to agree that her manager behaved badly. You are checking your understanding, not judging a person you have never met.
Your suggestions may become useful later. If she asks for them, offer one and explore it together rather than handing her a complete list. She may also want a different response on a different day. Treat her answer as guidance for this conversation, not as a permanent rule about your friendship.
q: What is the primary aim of this reply?
choices: To evaluate the fairness of a work schedule.
To help a reader respond to a troubled friend.
To recommend a way to select weekend jobs.
To explain how managers can prevent complaints.
explain: 回覆說明如何確認朋友當下需要的支持，目的是改善回應方式。「評估班表公平」只是來信背景，回覆者沒有判定主管對錯。

To the Activities Committee: I recommend moving our board-game afternoon from the town hall to the school library. We booked the hall expecting sixty guests, but only twenty-four have registered. These tasks will take time, but two members have already offered to handle them.
Please compare the remaining costs and the inconvenience to guests before voting. If new registrations exceed the library's capacity, we should review the plan. The deposit deserves a place in our financial report; it should not, by itself, choose the room for us.

Registration should end before a room is booked.
Future costs and needs should guide the choice.

Interviewer: You lead a community baking class. What surprised you when you first taught beginners? Instructor: I could make a loaf without checking a recipe, so I thought explaining it would be easy. Then a student asked what I meant by "a warm place." I had pointed toward a corner of the room, but she wanted to know how to judge a suitable place in her own kitchen.
Interviewer: How did you respond? Instructor: I began listing the details I used without noticing them. I also watched a beginner follow my written directions while I remained quiet. When he stopped, I marked the point in my notes instead of reaching over to finish the step. Otherwise, I would have hidden the gap in my explanation.
Interviewer: Did you add every possible detail? Instructor: No. A page crowded with warnings can be difficult to use. I ask a new reader to try the directions, then add information where it is needed. Experienced bakers still have a role: they check that my simplified language has not changed the process. I need readers with different kinds of knowledge.
Interviewer: Has teaching changed what you take for granted? Instructor: Yes. Knowing a process and describing it are separate achievements. I still want my students to make good bread, but their questions are useful to me before the loaves come out of the oven. A pause at the table may tell me more about my instructions than a perfect loaf I helped them finish.
q: What is the central focus of the interview?
choices: How experienced bakers select reliable recipes
Why adding warnings makes recipes easier to use
How an expert learns to give usable instructions
Why beginners learn by watching expert bakers
explain: 各段圍繞講師如何發現知識落差、試用並修訂說明，重點是讓指示能用。「增加警語」只取局部，而且第三段明說過多警語可能難用。

Every Friday, Eli left the school radio room while I was still working. As the final song played, I filed the requests and put away the spare cables. He returned just as I switched off the equipment. He was usually reserved, and I had stopped asking where he went. By the third week, I had privately decided that he preferred a walk to the dull part of our job.
That afternoon, I stepped into the corridor to return a borrowed chair. Near the stairs, Eli stood with his head tilted toward a speaker. The music was barely audible, though it had sounded clear through my headphones. He wrote something on a small card. "It fades here," he said. He showed me other cards, each with a location and a time. The teacher had asked him to check the older speakers during our broadcasts. In the empty corridor, he could hear problems that passing students might otherwise cover with their voices.
Back in the radio room, I opened the duty sheet. It listed my closing tasks in careful detail. Beside Eli's name, there was one word: "sound." I had filled that short word with an entire story about him. Before the next broadcast, I asked him to add his checking route to the sheet. Then I wrote down the tasks each of us did out of the other's sight.
q: Which title best captures the story?
choices: The Final Song That Failed to Reach Its Audience
Two Radio Workers Disagree over Closing Duties
A Weekly Program Loses Its Most Helpful Worker
A Duty Sheet Leaves Part of the Story Untold
explain: 工作表只寫 sound，讓敘事者誤判 Eli，結尾才補齊看不見的工作。「最後一首歌傳不出去」誇大局部音量問題，也忽略人際理解的主線。

At Rillstone Quarry, the main attraction is an absence: a vast space where a hill once stood. The former stone works has no restored village or rows of souvenir shops. Instead, visitors follow the cut walls to see the marks left by different tools. In the afternoon, low sunlight makes those marks easier to see. A small shelter near the entrance explains how to recognize them, so it is worth stopping there before you walk.
Two routes explore the quarry. The lower path is broad and level, with benches placed along it. The upper route climbs a steep stairway to a ledge. Visitors can take this route only with a local guide on weekend mornings, stopping at places from which workers once lowered stone. The views from the ledge are wider, but the marks in the walls can be studied just as well from below.
Allow for a full afternoon if you choose the lower path and want time to sketch or read the shelter's notes. Food is not sold inside, though drinking water is available at the entrance. Visitors seeking an exciting climbing challenge may find the pace slow. For those who enjoy noticing small details, however, the quarry turns an ordinary walk into a quiet lesson in how people have changed the land.

Nora Chen spent years as a badminton singles player, measuring a good match by the points she won. When her club asked her to try doubles, she brought the same habit with her. She chased shots her partner was ready to return and left open spaces behind her. During practice, the coach counted a rally as successful only when both players had covered their assigned areas. Gradually, Nora learned that leaving a shot to someone else could be the better decision.
Across town, stage designer Leo Wu faced a similar problem. His early sets were full of bright color and moving parts. Audiences remembered the scenery but sometimes missed the actor standing in front of it. Leo began watching rehearsals from the back row. In one production, he removed a large painted screen, making a small movement by the lead actor stand out. The scene gained force as the set grew simpler.
Neither Nora nor Leo has given up personal skill. Nora still practices difficult shots, and Leo still puts new visual ideas to the test. But both now keep some of their ability in reserve, using it when the shared task calls for it. Their experience suggests that a contribution should be judged by what it makes possible for others, as well as by how much attention it wins for its maker.
q: How are the first two paragraphs related?
choices: They trace two stages in one person's career.
They present similar lessons in different fields.
They compare two approaches to sports coaching.
They contrast a player's aims with a designer's.
